title: The servant who argues
hookLine: a servant who serves while arguing proudly loses the master's favor (Asa di Var M2, ang 474)

lines: A SIGH, A SPEECH, A LIST.
cards: You ask someone at home to take out the trash. They do it. Eventually.

But first there's a sigh, then a speech about how they always do everything, then a list of what you haven't done, then the bag dragged slowly to the door. The job is done. And somehow nobody in the house feels better.
Guru Angad, the second Guru, wrote a short salok about exactly this: service with an argument attached.

teach.h: PRIDE AND ARGUMENT AROUND THE WORK.
teach.b: The salok is marked mahala 2, Guru Angad's, on ang 474. In paraphrase: a servant who works for a master, but serves with pride and argues, who talks a great deal, doesn't win the master's pleasure.
One who loses the self and serves gains some honor. And the last line: Nanak, the one who clings to the Master meets the Master; that clinging is accepted. Notice what the arguing servant does right.
He shows up. He does the work. The salok doesn't call him lazy.
The problem is what he wraps around the work: gaarab, pride, and vaad, argument. Endless talk about how hard it is, how unfair, how much better he'd do it if he were in charge.

teach.h: THE JOB DONE, THE SERVICE NOT.
teach.b: The job gets done, but the service doesn't arrive, because service isn't only an action.
It's a way of offering it. On day five hundred forty-five, in Guru Nanak's pauri, the contented servants served and were accepted.
This salok, his successor's, shows the shadow side of the same picture: the proud served too, and argued, and lost the favor.
Sikhs tell a story about Guru Angad himself, when he was still called Bhai Lehna. Guru Nanak asked for hard and dirty jobs to be done, and while others objected, Lehna simply did them.
Tradition holds that's part of why Guru Nanak chose him.
Whatever the details, the salok reads like it came from someone who had lived it: serving without the speech.

how: Sikhs hear Guru Angad's salok on the arguing servant in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and Sikh seva is meant to be done humbly, without complaint or display.

o: pride that sours the service you give
anger at a master for unfair work
a servant's wages, paid at day's end

p: the one who loses the self

s: the arguing servant in the salok refuses to work
he does the work; the problem is the pride and argument around it.
this salok is marked mahala 2, Guru Angad's
it sits in the Asa di Var on ang 474.
the salok says one who loses the self in service gains honor
and the one who clings to the Master meets the Master.

games.q: you're Bhai Lehna, and Guru Nanak asks for a hard, dirty job to be done. others object. what do you do?
o: explain why someone else should do it.
do it, and remind everyone afterward.
games.why: tradition holds that Lehna simply did what was asked, and that this is part of why Guru Nanak chose him as the second Guru.

practice: Think of one task waiting for you that you'd normally do with a sigh: a chore, an errand, a request from someone.

Picture doing it all the way through with no commentary, no list, no speech in your head, just the work, offered; if something in you resists, let it, and breathe. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you picture finishing.

wordCard.voice: Gaarab, pride: in Guru Angad's salok, one who serves with gaarab and argument doesn't please the Master; one who loses the self in service gains honor.

carryVoice: Your line: serve without argument. The job and the service aren't always the same thing. Day five hundred fifty-nine, done.

sources.ref: Asa di Var, salok M2 (chaakar lagai chaakaree), Ang 474
